title: Why web apps feel slow: measuring server latency with percentiles
description: Your average response time is 120 ms, and your users are still unhappy. This quiz explains the gap: what latency data really looks like, which numbers you can safely combine, and why a server that is 90% busy is much slower than one that is 80% busy.

questions.title: Your service's p99 latency for the last hour is 250 ms. What does that number mean?

options.text: 99% of requests in that hour finished in 250 ms or less. Up to 1% took longer.
The typical request takes 250 ms.
No request in that hour took longer than 250 ms.
99% of requests took at least 250 ms.

questions.explanation: A percentile is a rank. Sort every request from that hour by latency, and p99 is the value 99% of the way down the list. So 99% of requests finished in 250 ms or less, and up to 1% took longer. It says nothing about the typical request (the median is closer to that), and it allows a slow tail above it. It also depends on the time window. "p99 for the last hour" and "p99 for the last week" come from different sets of requests, even if both read 250 ms.

questions.title: Over the same hour, Server A reports a p99 of 100 ms and Server B reports a p99 of 300 ms. If you combine their traffic, what is the combined p99?
questions.description: Both servers handled the same number of requests.

options.text: Somewhere between 100 and 300 ms. You can't get the exact value from the two p99s alone.
200 ms, the average of the two p99s.
400 ms, the sum of the two p99s.
300 ms, because the slower server always sets the combined p99.

questions.explanation: A percentile comes from the shape of a whole distribution, so you can't do arithmetic on two percentiles and get a third. The combined p99 lands between the two values, but where exactly depends on what each server's slowest requests look like. If Server B's slow tail is long and heavy, the combined p99 sits close to 300 ms. If it's short, the combined p99 can be much closer to 100 ms. To get the real number, recompute it from the combined data: raw request times, or histograms that use the same buckets.

questions.title: A dashboard shows a p99 for each of the last 24 hours. The hourly values range from 200 ms to 900 ms, and their average is 350 ms. Is the daily p99 350 ms?

options.text: Not necessarily. You have to recompute the daily p99 from the whole day's data. It isn't the average of the hourly p99s, or any other simple combination of them.
Yes, the daily p99 is the average of the hourly p99s.
Yes, as long as every hour had the same amount of traffic.
No, the daily p99 always equals the highest hourly p99, 900 ms.

questions.explanation: This is the same mistake as combining two servers' percentiles, just across hours instead of servers. The daily p99 comes from all of the day's requests, and it depends on how the slow requests from each hour stack up. The hourly p99 numbers alone don't carry that information. To get the true daily p99, recompute it from raw data or from histograms that cover the whole day.

questions.title: Which of these numbers can you combine across two sources (two servers, or two time windows) by simply adding them?

options.text: Request counts
Total latency (the sum of all request times)
Histogram bucket counts
Percentiles such as p50, p95, or p99
Medians

questions.explanation: Counts, sums, and histogram bucket counts are totals. To merge two sources, you add the matching numbers. Percentiles and medians depend on the shape of the whole distribution, so you have to recompute them from the combined data. That's why monitoring tools store histograms instead of percentiles. Histograms merge safely across servers and time windows, and the tool computes percentiles from the merged histogram when you run a query.

questions.title: Your monitoring tool stores latency in histogram buckets (0 to 10 ms, 10 to 25 ms, 25 to 50 ms, and so on) instead of storing every request. What's true about a p99 computed from those buckets?

images.alt: A latency histogram with bars of different widths, with p50, p95, and p99 marked inside specific buckets rather than at exact values

options.text: It's an estimate. The real value could be anywhere inside the bucket that holds the 99th percentile, and wider buckets mean bigger possible errors.
It's exact, as long as the buckets are evenly spaced.
It always overestimates the real p99.
It always underestimates the real p99.

questions.explanation: A bucket tells you how many requests landed in it, not where inside it each one landed. To compute a percentile, the tool has to guess, usually by assuming the requests are spread evenly across the bucket. The error can't be bigger than the bucket's width, but it can go either way, depending on where the real requests clustered. That's why good histogram setups use narrow buckets in the latency range you care about most.

questions.title: Why is the slowest request you've seen (the maximum latency) worth watching, but usually a bad target for a service-level objective (SLO)?

options.text: It's a real request, but rare one-off events cause it: a garbage-collection pause, a cold cache, a network blip. So it jumps around a lot and doesn't show how the service normally behaves.
It isn't real. The maximum is usually a measurement error.
It's a bad target because in practice it's always infinite.
It's a bad target because a maximum only exists for finite datasets.

questions.explanation: The maximum is a real worst case, and a sudden change in it can reveal a new problem. As a health target, though, it's too sensitive. One unlucky retry, a slow TLS handshake, or a short scheduler hiccup can spike it when nothing is really wrong. It also tends to grow the more requests you collect. A target like p99 or p99.9 is steadier because it describes a fixed share of traffic instead of one extreme request.

questions.title: You want an accurate p99 across all 200 servers in your fleet. Which approaches give a correct answer?

options.text: Collect every request's latency from all servers, then compute p99 on the combined set.
Combine each server's histogram into one (all servers use the same buckets), then compute p99 from it.
Average the 200 servers' p99 values.
Take the highest of the 200 servers' p99 values.

questions.explanation: You need data you can add up: raw request times, or histograms with the same buckets. Then you compute the percentile from the combined result. Averaging the p99s, or taking the highest one, is the same mistake as combining two servers' or two hours' p99s. Once the data has been reduced to a percentile, no arithmetic brings back the true combined value.

questions.title: Latency data is usually right-skewed: nothing can be faster than zero, but a long tail of slow requests stretches to the right. What does that mean for the average (mean) compared to the median?

images.alt: A right-skewed latency distribution with the median marked near the peak and the mean marked further right, pulled toward the tail

options.text: The mean is higher than the median. A few very slow requests pull the average up, while most requests stay near the fast end.
The mean and median are always equal for latency data.
The median is higher than the mean.
Skew doesn't affect the mean or the median.

questions.explanation: The mean reacts to extreme values. A handful of five-second requests shift the average even among thousands of fast ones. The median is just the middle request in the sorted list, so it ignores how far the tail stretches. With latency data, the mean sits above the median, and the heavier the tail, the bigger the gap. That's how "average response time" can look fine while a real share of users wait a long time. The average blends the slow requests in and hides them.

questions.title: Most requests to a service hit a warm cache and finish in about 5 ms. The rest miss the cache and take about 200 ms. Why does a single percentile like p90 describe this service poorly?

images.alt: A latency distribution with two separate peaks: a tall narrow one near 5 ms for cache hits, and a shorter wider one near 200 ms for cache misses

options.text: One number can't tell you whether p90 sits just past the fast group or inside the slow group. Those are very different systems, and p90 alone hides which one you have.
A distribution with two peaks has no p90.
Percentiles only work for normally distributed data.
You should leave cache misses out of the calculation.

questions.explanation: The p90 still exists, because it's still a rank in the sorted list. But one number hides the fact that there are two groups of requests with different causes. Where p90 lands depends on the cache hit rate. If the hit rate drops a little, p90 can jump from 6 ms to 190 ms even though neither group got any slower. The chart shows a big regression, when really more requests are taking the slow path. Tracking the hit rate and each group's latency separately tells you much more.

questions.title: This week, p50 latency rose from 40 ms to 90 ms, but p99 stayed at 800 ms. What kind of problem does that usually point to?

options.text: Something is slowing down most requests, not just the slowest ones, because the change shows up in the middle of the distribution.
A rare problem affecting a tiny share of requests, such as one bad server.
Nothing changed, because p50 and p99 always move together.
The p99 measurement is broken, because p50 and p99 always move in the same direction.

questions.explanation: p50 shows what a typical request experiences. If p50 moves and p99 doesn't, the slowdown affects most traffic. The tail was probably already dominated by a separate cause that this change didn't touch. Look at the code every request runs: extra serialization, a call that became synchronous, a slower database query plan, or new middleware. A rare event like one unhealthy server or an occasional garbage-collection pause would move the tail and leave the median alone. The next question covers that opposite pattern.

questions.title: p50 latency stays at 40 ms, but p99 climbs from 300 ms to 1,200 ms. Which statements are true?

options.text: A small share of requests got much slower, while the typical request didn't change.
Likely causes include periodic pauses like garbage collection, a few unhealthy servers, or slow paths that only some requests take, such as cache misses or retries.
Most users aren't affected, even though the tail number looks alarming.
The median must be wrong, because a real slowdown would show up there too.

questions.explanation: This is the mirror image of the previous question. The median didn't move, so the problem is limited to some requests or comes and goes. It's still worth fixing, because those users are having a much worse time. But you search differently. Looking at the code every request runs won't help much. Look instead at the specific servers or code paths the slow requests go through.

questions.title: The chart below is a CDF (cumulative distribution function). Latency runs along the bottom, and the share of requests finished by that latency runs up the side, with lines marking p50, p95, and p99. What does a CDF make easier to read than a regular histogram?
questions.description: The chart shows latency data as a rising curve, with dashed lines marking p50, p95, and p99.

images.alt: A CDF curve rising from 0 to 1 as latency increases, with dashed lines showing where p50, p95, and p99 fall on the curve

options.text: What share of requests finished within a given latency. You can read percentiles straight off the curve.
Where the peaks of the distribution are.
The exact number of requests in each latency bucket.
The mean latency.

questions.explanation: A CDF shows how many requests have finished by each latency. To find p95, go up to 95% on the vertical axis, move across to the curve, and read the latency below that point. A histogram is better for seeing shape, such as how many peaks there are and how wide each one is. On a CDF, two peaks show up only as a small double bend that's easy to miss. Use a histogram to see the shape, and a CDF to read off a percentile.

questions.title: Which of these often cause a web service's latency to have two peaks instead of one?

options.text: Cache hits versus cache misses on the same endpoint
Requests that hit a garbage-collection pause versus requests that don't
New connections that need a TLS handshake versus reused connections
Requests routed to a nearby region versus a distant one
Random measurement noise with no underlying cause

questions.explanation: Each of the four correct answers is a real fork in the request path. Every request takes one of two routes, and the routes cost very different amounts of time. That split is what creates two separate peaks. Random noise around a single path gives you one peak with a tail. A second peak means you have two groups of requests, not noise.

questions.title: Loading a page makes 100 backend calls at the same time. Each call has a 1% chance of being slow (over its p99), independent of the others. What percentage of page loads hit at least one slow call?
questions.description: Round to the nearest whole percent.

images.alt: One page fanning out to many parallel backend calls, with one slow call highlighted and the page's total time set by that slow call

questions.explanation: The chance of at least one slow call is 1 − (the chance that no call is slow) = 1 − 0.99^100 ≈ 1 − 0.366 ≈ 63%. Each call is fast 99% of the time, but with 100 calls, most page loads hit at least one slow one. The more calls a page waits on, the worse its tail gets, even when every single service is fast.

questions.title: When a page waits on N backend calls running at the same time, the page takes as long as the slowest call, not the average one. What happens as N grows?

options.text: The page's tail latency gets worse. Even if each call is usually fast, the chance that at least one lands in its slow tail rises with N.
The page gets faster, because parallel calls average out each other's slowness.
N doesn't matter, because the calls run at the same time.
The page's median latency rises in proportion to N, as fast as the tail.

questions.explanation: The page waits for the slowest call, so adding calls can only keep that wait the same or make it longer. Each extra call is another chance to hit a slow one. The median changes slowly, because most calls finish near their usual time. The tail (p95, p99) changes much sooner, because one slow call out of many is enough to slow down the whole page.

questions.title: Why does a system's tail latency usually depend on its slowest dependency rather than its average one?

options.text: A request can't finish until every service it calls has responded, so it takes at least as long as whichever one was slowest for that request.
Slow dependencies are always called first.
Monitoring tools automatically average all dependencies together.
The fastest dependency's time gets subtracted from the total.

questions.explanation: Whether a request calls its dependencies one after another or all at once, it takes at least as long as the slowest one. A dependency with a good average can still dominate the tail, because the requests that catch it on a slow call become the slow requests. Making an already fast dependency faster on average barely moves p99. The tail improves when you fix the dependency with the worst tail, however good its average looks.

questions.title: A hedged request sends a duplicate request after a short delay and uses whichever response comes back first. Which statements about hedging and retries are true?

options.text: They can shorten the tail by giving a slow call a second, independent chance to finish quickly.
They add load to the backend, because some requests are handled twice.
They stop helping, or make things worse, when the backend is overloaded, because the extra requests arrive when there's no spare capacity.
They remove tail latency completely, with no downsides.

questions.explanation: Hedging works when slowness is random and independent, like a garbage-collection pause on one server or a brief network blip. The second attempt probably won't hit the same bad luck. It fails when the slowness has a shared cause, like overload. Duplicate requests add more load to a system that's already struggling, which is how retry storms start. Good hedging policies limit the extra load and switch off when error rates or latency point to a system-wide problem.

questions.title: Same setup, but now the page makes 20 backend calls instead of 100. Each still has an independent 1% chance of being slow. What percentage of page loads hit at least one slow call?
questions.description: Round to the nearest whole percent.
questions.explanation: 1 − 0.99^20 ≈ 1 − 0.818 ≈ 18%. With 100 calls it was about 63%. Making 5× fewer calls cut slow page loads by about 3.5×, not 5×, because the math isn't linear. With 100 calls, many page loads had more than one slow call, so removing calls doesn't remove slow pages one for one. Fewer calls still helps a lot: slow page loads drop from almost two in three to about one in five.

questions.title: Back to 100 backend calls. Hedging now cuts each call's chance of being slow from 1% to 0.1%. What percentage of page loads hit at least one slow call?
questions.explanation: 1 − 0.999^100 ≈ 1 − 0.905 ≈ 9.5%. Making each call 10× less likely to be slow cut slow page loads from about 63% to about 9.5%, roughly 6.6×, not 10×. The reason is the same as in the last question: at 1% per call, many page loads had several slow calls at once. To improve further, also reduce the number of calls the page waits on.

questions.title: Little's Law connects three averages: the number of requests in a system (L), the rate at which requests arrive (λ), and the time each request spends in the system (W). Which equation is it?

images.alt: A box labeled 'system' with requests arriving at rate lambda, L requests in progress inside the box, and requests leaving after an average time W

options.text: L = λW
L = λ / W
W = λL
λ = LW

questions.explanation: The average number of requests in a system equals the arrival rate times the average time each request spends there. It holds for any stable system, whatever the traffic pattern, the time each request takes, or the number of servers. If you measure any two of L, λ, and W, you can calculate the third.

questions.title: A service handles 200 requests per second on average (λ) and has 50 requests in progress at any moment on average (L). Using Little's Law, how long does each request spend in the system on average (W), in milliseconds?
questions.explanation: W = L / λ = 50 / 200 per second = 0.25 seconds = 250 ms. This lets you estimate latency from concurrency and throughput when you don't measure latency directly. It's also a good sanity check for a latency number you do measure.

questions.title: A service handles 500 requests per second on average (λ), and each request takes 100 ms on average (W). Using Little's Law, how many requests are in progress at any moment on average (L)?
questions.explanation: L = λW = 500 per second × 0.1 seconds = 50. You use this direction for capacity planning. Given a target throughput and an expected latency, Little's Law tells you how much concurrency you need: in-flight requests, open connections, worker threads, or whatever holds a request while the system works on it.

questions.title: The chart below plots the average time requests wait in a queue against how busy the server is (utilization, ρ), with points at 50%, 80%, 90%, and 95%. What happens to wait time as utilization rises from 80% to 90% to 95%?
questions.description: The chart shows queue wait time against utilization from 0 to 100%, with points at 50%, 80%, 90%, and 95%.

images.alt: A line chart of queue wait time against server utilization from 0 to 100%, curving sharply upward as utilization approaches 100%, with points at 50%, 80%, 90%, and 95%

options.text: It grows much faster than a straight line. Each extra point of utilization adds more wait than the one before, especially past about 80%.
It grows at the same steady rate, whatever the starting utilization.
It stays flat until 100%, then jumps suddenly with no warning.
It goes down, because a busier server wastes less time per request.

questions.explanation: For a simple single-server queue, wait time grows with ρ / (1 − ρ), which heads toward infinity as ρ approaches 1. Going from 50% to 80% busy takes that factor from 1 to 4. Going from 80% to 95% takes it from 4 to 19, almost 5× worse, for a smaller jump in utilization. That's the hockey-stick shape. The closer a server runs to full capacity, the more each bit of extra load costs in wait time, long before it reaches 100%.

questions.title: Using ρ / (1 − ρ) as a relative measure of queueing delay (higher means longer waits), what is its value at ρ = 0.95?
questions.explanation: 0.95 / (1 − 0.95) = 0.95 / 0.05 = 19. At 80% utilization the factor is 0.8 / 0.2 = 4, and at 50% it's 0.5 / 0.5 = 1. Once a server is more than about 70 to 80% busy, equal steps in utilization cause much bigger steps in delay.

questions.title: A system has exactly enough capacity for its average traffic and nothing more. Why does it tend to break down, not just slow down a little, when traffic reaches about 2× the average?

options.text: Real traffic comes in bursts. Bursts push utilization toward 100%, where wait time grows much faster than load.
With no spare capacity, even short bursts create a backlog the system can't absorb.
When requests arrive faster than the system can handle them for any length of time, the queue keeps growing. The system falls behind and stays behind.
The system's capacity automatically doubles when traffic reaches 2× the average.

questions.explanation: A system sized for its average load runs near 100% utilization whenever traffic is above average. That's exactly where, according to ρ / (1 − ρ), a little more load adds a lot of waiting. At 2× the average, requests arrive faster than the system can finish them (ρ is above 1). Work piles up faster than it drains, and the backlog keeps growing, along with the latency of everything stuck in it, until traffic drops or you add capacity. That's why teams leave plenty of headroom above the average load.

questions.title: Two systems are both 80% busy on average and have the same average time per request. In one, request times vary a lot: some take 1 ms, others 500 ms. In the other, every request takes about the same time. Which statements are true?

options.text: The system with variable request times has longer average waits, even though its utilization and average request time match the other system's.
Variability in request times, or in the gaps between arrivals, adds waiting on top of what utilization alone predicts.
That's why approximations like Kingman's formula include a variability term, not just the utilization term ρ / (1 − ρ).
Both systems have the same average utilization, so they must have the same average wait.

questions.explanation: Wait time depends on more than how busy a server is. With variable request times, the server is sometimes idle and sometimes stuck behind a pile of slow work, and that pile takes a long time to clear. Steady, predictable work at the same average rate doesn't pile up the same way. Kingman's formula captures this: variability multiplies the delay that utilization causes. Two systems with the same numbers on paper can have very different wait times in practice.

questions.title: Ten servers each have their own queue. Alternatively, the same ten servers share one queue, and the next free server takes the next waiting request. With the same total traffic and the same server speed, which setup has shorter average waits, and why?

images.alt: Two panels: on the left, ten separate queues of uneven length, each feeding its own server; on the right, one shared snaking queue feeding the same ten servers

options.text: The shared queue. No request gets stuck behind a long line while another server sits idle.
The ten separate queues. Small queues always clear faster than one big one.
They're the same, because total traffic and total capacity are the same.
The ten separate queues. A shared queue creates contention that slows every server down.

questions.explanation: With ten separate queues, some lines get a run of arrivals by chance while others sit empty. A request that joined a long line keeps waiting even though a server two lines over is free. A shared queue removes that bad luck, because the next free server always takes the next request. The ten servers act like one big server instead of ten small ones, so average waits are shorter. It's the same reason one snaking line at a store usually moves faster than several separate lines.

questions.title: An app can group several writes into one database call. Bigger batches mean fewer, more efficient calls (higher throughput), but each item waits longer for its batch to fill (higher latency). Where is the best batch size usually?

options.text: Where a bigger batch stops adding enough throughput to be worth the extra latency. For many workloads that's a fairly small batch or a short time limit, not the largest batch the system can hold.
Always the largest batch the system can hold, because bigger batches are always better.
Always a batch size of one, because batching never helps.
Nowhere. Throughput and latency don't trade off in batching.

questions.explanation: The throughput gains from batching shrink fast. Going from 1 to 10 items per call helps a lot, because it spreads the fixed cost of each call. Going from 1,000 to 2,000 barely helps, because that cost is already spread thin. Meanwhile, the latency cost keeps growing with every extra item you wait for. That's why batch writers usually set two limits: send the batch when it's full or when a maximum wait time passes, whichever comes first. The size limit captures most of the throughput gain, and the time limit caps how long any single item waits.

questions.title: The timeline below compares the evenly spaced requests a load tester planned to send with the requests it actually sent while the service froze for a while. Based on that gap, what is coordinated omission?
questions.description: The chart shows the planned, evenly spaced requests above the requests the load tester actually sent, with a gap where it sent nothing during the freeze.

images.alt: Two timelines: an evenly spaced planned request schedule on top, and the load tester's actual requests below it, which stop completely during a service freeze and then resume

options.text: A load tester that waits for each response before sending the next request stops sending during a freeze. The requests that would have measured the freeze are exactly the ones that never get sent.
A bug where the load tester sends too many requests at once and overloads the service.
A way of scheduling requests across several load testers.
A measurement technique that skips slow requests on purpose to keep results clean.

questions.explanation: A simple load tester sends request N+1 only after it gets the response to request N. If the service freezes for five seconds, the tester just waits. It doesn't send the requests it should have sent during those five seconds. The requests it sends after the freeze see normal latency, so the freeze barely shows up in the results. Gil Tene named this effect. The missing requests line up ("coordinate") with the freeze they should have measured, so they get left out instead of being recorded as slow.

questions.title: A load tester waits for each response before sending the next request. What does coordinated omission do to the latency percentiles it reports?

options.text: It makes the tail look better than it is. Real users, who don't wait for each other, would see worse latency during a freeze.
It makes the tail look worse than it is.
It only affects throughput numbers, not percentiles.
It only affects the mean, never the percentiles.

questions.explanation: The missing requests are the ones that would have recorded the worst latencies. Real users don't wait for each other's requests to finish. In production, requests keep arriving during a freeze, pile up, and get served late once it ends. The load tester never sent those requests, so they're missing from its results. The reported p99, and in a long freeze even the p50, looks better than what real traffic would show. To fix this, use a load tester that sends requests on a fixed schedule whether or not earlier responses have come back, or one that corrects its results for the requests it skipped.

questions.title: For the same request, the server logs 40 ms of processing time, but the browser measures 180 ms from the click to the response. What does that 140 ms gap most likely contain?

options.text: Time outside the server's code: network travel, DNS lookup and TLS setup, waiting at a load balancer or proxy, and waiting before the server's code started.
Clock differences between the browser and the server, which are usually hundreds of milliseconds.
Nothing real. A gap like this is always a measurement bug.
Time the browser spent rendering the response, which should always be left out of latency numbers.

questions.explanation: Server-side timing only covers the code the team chose to measure, usually starting once the request reaches the application. It misses everything before that: the DNS lookup, the TCP and TLS handshakes, network travel both ways, and time queued at a load balancer or proxy. That gap is real, and it's often most of what users feel. That's why "our server's p99 is fast" and "our users see fast pages" can be very different claims. To see the full picture, also measure in the browser, for example with real-user monitoring.

questions.title: Why does a latency SLO need both a time window, like "over any rolling 30 days", and a target, like "p99 under 500 ms", instead of just a number?

options.text: Without a window, the same target can be easy to meet or easy to miss depending on the time range. One bad minute looks very different in "p99 for the last minute" than in "p99 for the last 30 days".
The window is only there for legal or compliance reasons.
The target alone is enough. The window is optional.
Only throughput SLOs need a window, not latency SLOs.

questions.explanation: A percentile is computed over some set of requests, so "p99 under 500 ms" means nothing until you say which requests. A five-minute window during an outage gives a very different p99 than a 30-day window that includes the same outage. Both are correct answers to different questions. The window also decides how much a short bad stretch counts. A five-minute freeze barely changes a 30-day p99 but dominates a five-minute one. So choosing the window means choosing how much short-term pain the SLO tolerates.

questions.title: An SLO promises 99.9% availability over a rolling 30-day window. How many minutes of downtime does that allow in those 30 days?
questions.description: Round to one decimal place. (30 days = 43,200 minutes.)
questions.explanation: Allowed downtime = (1 − 0.999) × 43,200 minutes = 0.001 × 43,200 = 43.2 minutes. This is the SLO's error budget: how much unreliability it allows before it counts as broken. Turning a percentage into minutes makes it practical. A team can choose to spend some of those 43.2 minutes on a risky deploy or a planned migration, and they know how much room is left for surprises.
